screens.title: require(): Input validation that refunds gas
screens.narratorSegment: require is the standard tool for enforcing preconditions in Solidity functions. It evaluates a boolean condition and, if false, reverts the transaction while refunding the remaining gas to the caller. This makes require ideal for validating user input, permission checks, and conditions that may legitimately be false. For example, in a deposit function require(msg. value > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero") ensures only positive deposits proceed. The refund behavior means the caller doesn't lose the gas budget they didn't use, which is an important UX and cost consideration for users interacting with your contract. A useful tip is to include a concise message string to help off-chain tools and logs surface the reason for failure. That message is encoded in revert data and can be read by tools like Hardhat during testing. A common misconception is to use require where an internal invariant should be guaranteed by code — if the condition truly cannot be false, prefer assert instead. Also avoid overly long error strings for frequent checks because strings increase gas costs in revert data when used in many places. In short, require is your go-to for expected runtime checks that should stop execution and refund unused gas. How will you identify which checks belong behind require in your contracts?

keyIdea.title: require in one line
keyIdea.text: Use require for expected user-facing checks; it reverts and refunds unused gas, and supports a human-readable message for debugging.

content.html:
Core Concept › require()

Definition and intent

require evaluates a condition and reverts with a message if false, returning remaining gas to the caller.

  • • Best for validating inputs, permissions, and expected external conditions.
  • • Includes optional string message for off-chain debugging.
  • • Refunds remaining gas when it reverts; better UX for callers.
Common mistake
Using require for internal invariants that should never fail wastes clarity and may hide bugs. Use assert for those cases.
Code example
// deposit function
function deposit() public payable {
  require(msg.value > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero");
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
}
This enforces a positive deposit and ensures the caller is not charged for unused gas when the check fails. Include concise messages to make test output and logs clearer.
Analogy
require acts like a door guard checking tickets; if the ticket is invalid, the visitor gets turned away but doesn't pay extra fees.
Key Takeaway
Use require for expected, recoverable checks that should refund unused gas and provide a message for debugging.

screens.title: revert(): explicit control and complex conditions
screens.narratorSegment: revert is a primitive that explicitly aborts execution and returns remaining gas to the caller, similar to require. Its main advantage is flexibility: revert can appear inside if statements or deeper logic branches so you can compose complex condition checks before deciding to abort. In practice require(condition, message) is shorthand for if (! condition) revert(message), but using revert directly can make longer validation branches clearer and easier to read. For example, you might check multiple interdependent conditions in a function and call revert with different messages depending on which check fails. An important pattern is to favor concise revert messages or, better yet, custom errors for frequently used failure modes to save gas. Another common misconception is thinking revert behaves like assert; it does not consume all remaining gas. Instead revert and require both refund unused gas. Use revert when you need detailed conditional logic or want to consolidate multiple failure points in a single control flow block. Finally, remember to keep messages compact and consistent so tests and off-chain tooling can parse failures reliably. How would you structure complex validation so each path reports a clear reason?

keyIdea.text: Use revert for explicit, conditional aborts inside complex control flow; prefer concise messages or custom errors for gas efficiency.

content.html:
Core Concept › revert()

Why use revert

revert gives explicit control to abort execution inside arbitrary control flow. It refunds unused gas like require but is more flexible for complex validations.

  • • Use revert inside if statements when multiple dependent checks determine failure reasons.
  • • Prefer short messages or custom errors when repeated across the contract to reduce gas cost.
  • • revert does not indicate an internal bug — it signals an expected failure scenario.
Misconception
Do not assume revert consumes all gas like assert. It refunds remaining gas and should be treated as a recoverable failure signal for expected conditions.
Example
function withdrawWithRevert(uint _amount) public {
  if (balances[msg.sender] < _amount) {
    revert("Insufficient balance for withdrawal");
  }
  if (_amount == 0) {
    revert("Withdraw amount must be positive");
  }
  balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
  payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);
}
This style groups distinct failure reasons with clear text; use custom errors when this pattern repeats frequently to save gas.
Pro tip
Refactor repeated revert messages into custom errors for production to lower transaction costs and make tests precise.

screens.title: assert(): internal invariants and bug signals
screens.narratorSegment: assert is intended for internal sanity checks and invariants that indicate a contract logic bug if violated. When assert fails, it consumes all remaining gas and signals a severe issue within the contract itself. In modern Solidity (0.8+), arithmetic overflow or underflow already reverts automatically, so using assert for overflow checks is largely unnecessary. Instead, assert is best used to verify correctness after complex internal calculations or to ensure that an unavoidable invariant holds. For example, after a set of transformations you might assert that total supply hasn't changed unexpectedly. A frequent mistake is to use assert for user-facing conditions such as checking input values or caller permissions. That misuse punishes the caller with lost gas and obscures the real problem. Always choose require or revert for expected external failures. Another useful guideline is to include internal comments explaining why the invariant must always hold, so future maintainers understand that an assert failure points to a bug in logic, not user error. In tests, assert failures are rare but should trigger immediate debugging. What invariant in your contract would you protect with assert, and why must it never be false?

keyIdea.title: assert in one line

content.html:
Definition › assert()

When assert makes sense

Assert checks are reserved for conditions that should be true by construction. Their failure implies a code bug, not invalid input.

  • • Use for internal invariants after complex computations.
  • • In Solidity 0.8+, arithmetic overflow checks are automatic, reducing the need for assert for maths.
  • • Failed assert consumes all remaining gas — a deliberate loud signal.
Example pattern
function processCriticalState(uint _value) internal {
  uint newCalculatedValue = _value * 2;
  assert(newCalculatedValue >= _value);
}
Here assert checks a mathematical property that should hold; if it fails, investigate the calculation logic rather than blaming user input.
Common mistake
Using assert for input validation leads to unnecessary gas loss and poor diagnostics. Prefer require or custom errors for expected failures.

screens.title: Custom Errors: compact, typed failure reporting
screens.narratorSegment: Custom errors introduced in Solidity 0.8.4 let you define named error types with parameters, producing much smaller revert payloads than long strings. Instead of revert("Insufficient balance: requested x, available y"), you define error InsufficientBalance(uint requested, uint available) and revert InsufficientBalance(requested, available). The revert encoding then includes only the error selector and parameters, which decreases gas and makes it easier for off-chain tools to identify the exact failure type programmatically. Custom errors are particularly useful in frequently-called functions or when your contract needs to return precise diagnostic data to tests and tooling. When designing custom errors, choose clear names and minimal parameter sets that provide actionable context without logging sensitive data. For example, ZeroAmount() and InsufficientBalance(uint requested, uint available) are expressive and compact. A common misconception is that strings are always fine; in production they can inflate gas costs for repeated failures. Use custom errors for widely used checks and keep string messages for one-off debugging during development. Now consider which failure modes in your contract benefit most from a typed error versus a short message. Custom Errors: compact, typed failure reporting means define error types with parameters and revert with them to reduce revert data size and enable machine-readable failure types.. In practical terms, define and revert custom errors to save gas and provide structured data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Custom Errors

Why custom errors

Custom errors return an identifier and parameters instead of lengthy strings, saving gas and enabling precise test assertions.

  • • Define with the error keyword and use revert ErrorName(params).
  • • Cheaper than string messages when errors occur often.
  • • Better for automated tooling to match specific failure types.
Design advice
Keep parameters minimal and avoid logging sensitive information in error parameters. Choose expressive names so tests and logs remain readable.
Code walkthrough
error InsufficientBalance(uint requested, uint available);
error ZeroAmount();

function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
  if (balances[msg.sender] < _amount) {
    revert InsufficientBalance(_amount, balances[msg.sender]);
  }
  if (_amount == 0) {
    revert ZeroAmount();
  }
  // continue...
Off-chain tools can decode the error selector and parameters, making it straightforward to react or surface a short message to users.
Analogy
Custom errors are like typed exceptions in other languages — they carry structured information without long text blobs.

screens.title: Events and emit: logging for off-chain clients
screens.narratorSegment: Events let contracts write compact logs to transaction receipts. Unlike storage, event data is not part of the contract's state; it appears in the transaction's log and is cheaper than saving the same data on-chain. Off-chain applications, block explorers, and indexing services listen for events and update UIs or perform analytics in near real-time. Events are declared with the event keyword and emitted with emit. Use indexed parameters on up to three fields so external clients can filter quickly by address, id, or another frequently searched parameter. A practical example is a Deposit event that records depositor, amount, and new balance. Frontends can subscribe to Deposit and update dashboards without polling the contract for balances. However, events are public history — don’t emit secrets. Also, be deliberate about which fields to index: indexing increases log size and gas, so index only fields commonly filtered in queries. Finally, consider emission timing: emit after a successful state change to ensure logs aren’t misleading if subsequent operations revert. How will your dApp consume events to deliver a responsive user experience? Events and emit: logging for off-chain clients means emit events to log significant state changes; use indexed fields for efficient off-chain filtering and avoid putting secrets into logs.. In practical terms, use events to signal state changes without storing on-chain state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Events & emit

What events are for

Events log information for off-chain systems. They are cheaper than on-chain storage and are indexable for efficient queries.

  • • Declare with event and write with emit.
  • • Up to three parameters can be indexed to enable fast filtering by off-chain clients.
  • • Do not put secret data in events; logs are public forever.
Emission timing
Emit after successful state changes to avoid logging an action that later reverts; for ownership transfers you may emit previous and new owner to record context.
Event example
event Deposit(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);

function deposit() public payable {
  require(msg.value > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero");
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value, balances[msg.sender]);
}
A frontend can listen for Deposit events to update UI immediately when new deposits happen without polling balances constantly.
Why it matters
Events make your contract observable and integrate it with UIs and indexes efficiently while keeping on-chain state smaller and cheaper.

screens.title: Indexed event parameters and filtering
screens.narratorSegment: Indexed parameters in events let off-chain clients filter logs by field values without scanning every transaction payload. Solidity allows up to three indexed parameters per event; these indexed fields go into the bloom filter, which nodes and clients use to match logs quickly. A typical pattern is to index addresses and identifiers that frontends frequently query — for example, index depositor and beneficiary in an Escrow contract so a UI can ask, "Show me all deposits or releases involving this address." When choosing indexed fields, prefer values you expect frontends or analytics to search by. Avoid indexing large or rarely-searched data because indexing increases gas costs. Also remember that not all parameters should be indexed: keep sensitive information out of indexed fields and logs altogether. A subtle point is that indexed parameters are stored differently and may be hashed for dynamic types. For strings or arrays, the indexed value often becomes a hash in the filter. Finally, design your events with consistent field order to simplify parsing and ensure your client libraries know whether fields are indexed or not. What three fields would you index for your most common queries?

keyIdea.title: Indexed fields
keyIdea.text: Index up to three high-value query fields like addresses or IDs so off-chain clients can filter efficiently while keeping gas costs reasonable.

content.html:
Process Flow › Indexed event parameters

Choosing indexed fields

Indexed parameters allow efficient on-chain log filtering. Limit to three fields and pick ones you expect UIs to query.

  1. Identify the most common search values (addresses, IDs).
  2. Index those fields to enable bloom-filtered queries.
  3. Avoid indexing sensitive or rarely used data to save gas.
Note on dynamic types
Strings and arrays when indexed are represented by their hash in the logs, so plan client decoding accordingly.
Example event
event FundsDeposited(address indexed depositor, address indexed beneficiary, uint amount);

// Depositor and beneficiary are good indexed fields for filtering by user address.
A UI can ask a node for logs where depositor equals a given address, returning only relevant transactions quickly.
Quick checklist
Index fields you will query; limit to three; avoid secrets; plan for hashed dynamic types.

screens.title: Gas implications and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding gas implications helps you choose the most efficient error reporting in production. require and revert both revert execution and refund unused gas; they are appropriate for expected user-facing failures. However, using string messages repeatedly across functions can increase transaction size and raise gas costs when failures occur. Custom errors are more gas-efficient because they encode a selector and parameters rather than full strings. That efficiency matters when failures are common or messages are long. assert is different: it indicates an internal bug and consumes all remaining gas when it fails, making failures loud and expensive. Use assert sparingly. Events also have gas costs: logs are cheaper than storage but are still not free. Keep event payloads minimal and index only commonly-filtered fields. A practical best practice is to use require or revert with short messages during development, then refactor frequent failure messages into custom errors before production, and always emit concise events. Tests should assert both expected reverts and emitted events so you can measure gas and confirm behavior. Which parts of your contract will you measure and optimize for gas?

keyIdea.title: Gas rules
keyIdea.text: Prefer custom errors for frequent failures and keep event payloads minimal; reserve assert for rare internal faults.

content.html:
Comparison › Gas and best practices
require / revert
Refund remaining gas, good for input validation. Short messages ok in dev; refactor repeated messages to custom errors for production.
assert
Signals internal bug; consumes remaining gas. Use sparingly and document the invariant clearly.
Custom Errors
Lower revert data gas cost and provide structured parameters for tests and tooling.
Events
Cheaper than storage but still cost gas. Keep payloads small and index only what you query.
Practical workflow
Use readable messages in dev; refactor to custom errors and concise events before deployment to optimize gas and observability.

screens.title: Order of operations: emit before or after state changes?
screens.narratorSegment: When designing events and state changes, deciding whether to emit before or after a state modification impacts how logs are interpreted. A common guideline is to emit events after state changes so logs reflect the final confirmed state. For example, after reducing a balance and transferring funds, emit Withdrawal with the new balance to show the finished state. However, some events like OwnershipTransferred are sometimes emitted before assignment so the event can include the previous owner as well as the new owner; both approaches are valid if used consistently and documented. Inconsistent timing can confuse users and make debugging harder: if you emit before the final update and a subsequent operation reverts, the log may suggest an action that didn't complete. Always design event order to match how off-chain clients expect to reconstruct state and be explicit in your contract comments. For critical flows, include a test that checks both the state and the emitted event in the same transaction to ensure they align. Finally, if you must emit prior to a state change for context, ensure the event communicates that and include both old and new values when helpful. What emission timing rule will you adopt across your contracts?

keyIdea.title: Emission order
keyIdea.text: Prefer emitting events after state changes to reflect confirmed outcomes; if emitting before, include context and be consistent.

content.html:
Process Flow › Emit order

Guideline

Emit events after state changes to ensure logs reflect actual outcomes. If you emit before, include both old and new values for clarity.

• Emit after successful changes to avoid logging actions undone by reverts.
• For events showing a transition, include previous and current values for context.
• Document your pattern and write tests that assert state and logs together.
Example — Ownership transfer
function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public {
  require(_newOwner != address(0), "New owner cannot be zero address");
  emit OwnershipTransferred(owner, _newOwner);
  owner = _newOwner;
}
This example emits previous and new owner; consistent documentation clarifies the intended ordering for clients and auditors.
Check
Write tests that assert both the final state and the emitted event in the same transaction to ensure alignment.

screens.title: Escrow Contract — state and roles
screens.narratorSegment: The Escrow contract is an excellent hands-on example to apply error handling and events. Start with clear state: depositor, beneficiary, arbiter, amount, and a boolean isReleased. The constructor assigns depositor to msg. sender and requires non-zero addresses for beneficiary and arbiter. These checks use require to validate input at deployment. Important invariants include that isReleased is false until funds are moved and that only the arbiter can release or refund the escrow. Protect these invariants using custom errors to provide compact, expressive failure signals such as NotArbiter and EscrowAlreadyReleased. Architecturally, keep the contract small and focused: deposit sets amount and emits FundsDeposited, release transfers the amount to beneficiary, sets isReleased to true and emits FundsReleased, and refund mirrors that flow back to the depositor. Remember to ensure correct order: change state before transfer where appropriate or vice versa based on reentrancy considerations and safety patterns. Document the role checks and event emission order so off-chain clients interpret logs correctly. As you implement, think about tests that assert that only the depositor can deposit and only the arbiter can trigger release or refund.

keyIdea.title: Escrow state
keyIdea.text: Define clear roles and state, use require/custom errors for role checks, and emit events on deposit, release, and refund for observability.

content.html:
Architecture › Escrow contract

State & roles

  • • depositor: address that creates the escrow and sends funds.
  • • beneficiary: address that receives funds on release.
  • • arbiter: trusted address that can release or refund funds.
  • • amount: the Ether held in escrow; isReleased: whether funds were moved.
Constructor checks
Use require to prevent zero addresses and assign depositor to msg.sender. These are deployment-time validations that immediately revert for invalid parameters.
Design note
Use custom errors for role violations and repeated checks to save gas in production.
State snapshot
address public depositor;
address public beneficiary;
address public arbiter;
uint public amount;
bool public isReleased;
Check your design
Which checks should revert with a message, and which should use custom errors for gas savings?

screens.title: Escrow functions: deposit, release, refund
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the deposit, release, and refund functions for a secure Escrow. The deposit function is payable and should only accept Ether from the depositor. Use a custom error NotDepositor(msg. sender) if msg. sender is not the depositor and ZeroAmount() if msg. value equals zero. After setting amount = msg. value, emit a FundsDeposited event with depositor, beneficiary, and amount. The release function must require that msg. sender is the arbiter and that the escrow is not already released; use NotArbiter and EscrowAlreadyReleased custom errors for clarity. Set isReleased to true and transfer the amount to beneficiary, then emit FundsReleased. The refund function mirrors release but sends funds back to the depositor and emits FundsRefunded. In implementation, checking and setting state before external calls helps limit reentrancy risks. Emit events to make the transitions observable for off-chain systems. Tests should assert that the correct custom error is reverted for invalid calls and that the proper event is emitted on success. By making errors typed and events indexed, you improve both gas efficiency and testability. Which of these checks will you unit-test first to build confidence?

keyIdea.title: Function pattern
keyIdea.text: Validate roles with custom errors, change state deterministically, perform transfers safely, and emit events to record outcomes.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Escrow functions

Starter code pattern

error NotArbiter(address caller);
error NotDepositor(address caller);
error EscrowAlreadyReleased();
error ZeroAmount();

event FundsDeposited(address indexed depositor, address indexed beneficiary, uint amount);

function deposit() public payable {
  if (msg.sender != depositor) revert NotDepositor(msg.sender);
  if (msg.value == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
  if (isReleased) revert EscrowAlreadyReleased();
  amount = msg.value;
  emit FundsDeposited(depositor, beneficiary, amount);
}
This pattern yields clear, gas-efficient errors and an event that frontends can consume.
Release / Refund
function release() public {
  if (msg.sender != arbiter) revert NotArbiter(msg.sender);
  if (isReleased) revert EscrowAlreadyReleased();
  isReleased = true;
  payable(beneficiary).transfer(amount);
  emit FundsReleased(arbiter, beneficiary, amount);
}

function refund() public {
  if (msg.sender != arbiter) revert NotArbiter(msg.sender);
  if (isReleased) revert EscrowAlreadyReleased();
  isReleased = true;
  payable(depositor).transfer(amount);
  emit FundsRefunded(arbiter, depositor, amount);
}
Testing tip
Assert custom errors in negative tests and check emitted events and state in positive tests to validate both behavior and observability.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: This section highlights frequent errors and how to avoid them. First, don't over-rely on assert for input checks. Using assert where user input could fail wastes gas and miscommunicates the nature of the failure. Second, don't omit error messages or custom errors — cryptic reverts make debugging and user support difficult. Third, avoid putting sensitive data in events; logs are public and permanent. Fourth, be mindful of event order: emitting an event before a state change that later reverts can mislead off-chain systems. Fifth, avoid indexing unnecessary fields; indexing increases gas costs and log size. A practical safety note is to test not only that functions succeed but that they fail with the correct custom error and emit the intended event when successful. When refactoring from string messages to custom errors, update tests to check for the error selector or use tooling that decodes custom error reverts. Also measure gas for hot paths: repeated revert messages or large event payloads can raise transaction costs over heavy usage. Finally, maintain consistent documentation for your event schema and error types so consumers and auditors can rely on stable signals. Which of these mistakes do you see most often in sample contracts you review?

keyIdea.text: Use require/revert for user errors, assert for invariants, custom errors for efficiency, and keep events concise, indexed thoughtfully, and ordered consistently.

content.html:
Common Mistakes › Safety notes

Frequent pitfalls

  • • Using assert for user-input validation — wastes gas and confuses failure semantics.
  • • Omitting clear error types or messages — slows debugging and hurts UX.
  • • Emitting secrets in events — logs are permanently public.
  • • Emitting events before final state changes — can produce misleading logs on reverts.
  • • Indexing too many or rarely-used fields — increases gas without real benefit.
Practical mitigation
Write tests that assert specific custom errors on negative cases, and verify emitted events and resulting state on positive cases. Measure gas for hot paths and refactor repeated strings into custom errors when needed.
Pro tip
Document error types and event schemas so consumers know what each log and revert means.
Check your tests
Include tests that expect both reverts with custom errors and precise event emissions to prevent regressions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas to remember. First, require and revert are your tools for expected input or permission checks and refund remaining gas on failure. Use them for user-facing validations. Second, assert is reserved for internal invariants that should never fail; a failure consumes remaining gas and indicates a bug. Third, custom errors give you compact, typed reverts that save gas and improve programmatic handling of failures. Fourth, events are the cost-effective way to communicate state changes to off-chain clients; index up to three fields and keep payloads concise. Finally, test both failures and logs: assert custom errors in negative tests and confirm emitted events and resulting state in positive flows. These practices together produce safer, cheaper, and more observable smart contracts. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will master the Solidity tools that make contracts robust and observable: require, revert, assert, custom errors, and events. We'll show you when each pattern is appropriate, how gas behavior differs between them, and why events are the efficient bridge from on-chain activity to off-chain dApps. You'll see concrete code examples that enforce input validation, signal internal invariants, and log state transitions for frontends. Smart contract errors don't behave like simple UI errors: an on-chain failure typically reverts the whole transaction. That means choosing the right mechanism affects both correctness and the gas returned to the caller. Later you'll implement an Escrow contract that uses custom errors for compact reporting and emits indexed events so UIs can filter activity. Along the way, you'll learn common mistakes — like overusing assert — and the practical order-of-operations to avoid misleading logs. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to pick the right error pattern for a given situation, design efficient custom errors, and use events correctly so your dApp can react reliably. Ready to explore the building blocks and trade-offs?

This chapter prepares you to select and apply Solidity error patterns and events with intent. First, you'll master require, revert, and assert so your contract responds correctly to invalid inputs or internal faults. That skill matters because a wrong choice can waste gas, hide bugs, or mislead off-chain listeners. Second, you'll learn gas implications and best practices. Understanding cost differences lets you make efficient decisions for production contracts and tests. Third, you'll design and use custom errors. These let you send structured, compact failure data to tools and tests, saving gas while improving debuggability. Finally, you'll implement events to communicate state changes to dApps. Proper event design—using indexed parameters, concise payloads, and consistent emission timing—helps frontends react without expensive state polling. Each objective is paired with a small visual mnemonic to help you remember when to use each pattern. As you work through the Escrow hands-on activity, you will apply these skills to a real contract, observing gas and logs in a test run. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like overusing assert or emitting sensitive data in events — these mistakes are explained and avoided throughout the lessons.

This second objectives screen focuses on application and verification. You will implement patterns in a hands-on Escrow contract: define custom errors like NotArbiter and ZeroAmount, emit events for deposit, release, and refund, and enforce correct caller checks to avoid accidental transfers. The practical aim is twofold: enforce safety at runtime and provide clear logs for off-chain systems. You'll also learn how to write tests that assert both revert reasons and emitted events. Testing custom errors and events helps ensure your contract fails clearly and your UI sees the same signal the chain records. You'll run through a sequence of actions in the lab: deposit by the depositor, release by the arbiter, and refund by the arbiter if necessary. Each function includes explicit checks and emits the appropriate event. This applied objective trains you to think about the contract not just as state but as a stream of logged events and deterministic failure modes. That perspective dramatically improves debugging, monitoring, and the user experience for dApps that consume your contract data.

require is the standard tool for enforcing preconditions in Solidity functions. It evaluates a boolean condition and, if false, reverts the transaction while refunding the remaining gas to the caller. This makes require ideal for validating user input, permission checks, and conditions that may legitimately be false. For example, in a deposit function require(msg. value > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero") ensures only positive deposits proceed. The refund behavior means the caller doesn't lose the gas budget they didn't use, which is an important UX and cost consideration for users interacting with your contract. A useful tip is to include a concise message string to help off-chain tools and logs surface the reason for failure. That message is encoded in revert data and can be read by tools like Hardhat during testing. A common misconception is to use require where an internal invariant should be guaranteed by code — if the condition truly cannot be false, prefer assert instead. Also avoid overly long error strings for frequent checks because strings increase gas costs in revert data when used in many places. In short, require is your go-to for expected runtime checks that should stop execution and refund unused gas. How will you identify which checks belong behind require in your contracts?

revert is a primitive that explicitly aborts execution and returns remaining gas to the caller, similar to require. Its main advantage is flexibility: revert can appear inside if statements or deeper logic branches so you can compose complex condition checks before deciding to abort. In practice require(condition, message) is shorthand for if (! condition) revert(message), but using revert directly can make longer validation branches clearer and easier to read. For example, you might check multiple interdependent conditions in a function and call revert with different messages depending on which check fails. An important pattern is to favor concise revert messages or, better yet, custom errors for frequently used failure modes to save gas. Another common misconception is thinking revert behaves like assert; it does not consume all remaining gas. Instead revert and require both refund unused gas. Use revert when you need detailed conditional logic or want to consolidate multiple failure points in a single control flow block. Finally, remember to keep messages compact and consistent so tests and off-chain tooling can parse failures reliably. How would you structure complex validation so each path reports a clear reason?

assert is intended for internal sanity checks and invariants that indicate a contract logic bug if violated. When assert fails, it consumes all remaining gas and signals a severe issue within the contract itself. In modern Solidity (0.8+), arithmetic overflow or underflow already reverts automatically, so using assert for overflow checks is largely unnecessary. Instead, assert is best used to verify correctness after complex internal calculations or to ensure that an unavoidable invariant holds. For example, after a set of transformations you might assert that total supply hasn't changed unexpectedly. A frequent mistake is to use assert for user-facing conditions such as checking input values or caller permissions. That misuse punishes the caller with lost gas and obscures the real problem. Always choose require or revert for expected external failures. Another useful guideline is to include internal comments explaining why the invariant must always hold, so future maintainers understand that an assert failure points to a bug in logic, not user error. In tests, assert failures are rare but should trigger immediate debugging. What invariant in your contract would you protect with assert, and why must it never be false?

Custom errors introduced in Solidity 0.8.4 let you define named error types with parameters, producing much smaller revert payloads than long strings. Instead of revert("Insufficient balance: requested x, available y"), you define error InsufficientBalance(uint requested, uint available) and revert InsufficientBalance(requested, available). The revert encoding then includes only the error selector and parameters, which decreases gas and makes it easier for off-chain tools to identify the exact failure type programmatically. Custom errors are particularly useful in frequently-called functions or when your contract needs to return precise diagnostic data to tests and tooling. When designing custom errors, choose clear names and minimal parameter sets that provide actionable context without logging sensitive data. For example, ZeroAmount() and InsufficientBalance(uint requested, uint available) are expressive and compact. A common misconception is that strings are always fine; in production they can inflate gas costs for repeated failures. Use custom errors for widely used checks and keep string messages for one-off debugging during development. Now consider which failure modes in your contract benefit most from a typed error versus a short message. Custom Errors: compact, typed failure reporting means define error types with parameters and revert with them to reduce revert data size and enable machine-readable failure types.. In practical terms, define and revert custom errors to save gas and provide structured data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Events let contracts write compact logs to transaction receipts. Unlike storage, event data is not part of the contract's state; it appears in the transaction's log and is cheaper than saving the same data on-chain. Off-chain applications, block explorers, and indexing services listen for events and update UIs or perform analytics in near real-time. Events are declared with the event keyword and emitted with emit. Use indexed parameters on up to three fields so external clients can filter quickly by address, id, or another frequently searched parameter. A practical example is a Deposit event that records depositor, amount, and new balance. Frontends can subscribe to Deposit and update dashboards without polling the contract for balances. However, events are public history — don’t emit secrets. Also, be deliberate about which fields to index: indexing increases log size and gas, so index only fields commonly filtered in queries. Finally, consider emission timing: emit after a successful state change to ensure logs aren’t misleading if subsequent operations revert. How will your dApp consume events to deliver a responsive user experience? Events and emit: logging for off-chain clients means emit events to log significant state changes; use indexed fields for efficient off-chain filtering and avoid putting secrets into logs.. In practical terms, use events to signal state changes without storing on-chain state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Indexed parameters in events let off-chain clients filter logs by field values without scanning every transaction payload. Solidity allows up to three indexed parameters per event; these indexed fields go into the bloom filter, which nodes and clients use to match logs quickly. A typical pattern is to index addresses and identifiers that frontends frequently query — for example, index depositor and beneficiary in an Escrow contract so a UI can ask, "Show me all deposits or releases involving this address." When choosing indexed fields, prefer values you expect frontends or analytics to search by. Avoid indexing large or rarely-searched data because indexing increases gas costs. Also remember that not all parameters should be indexed: keep sensitive information out of indexed fields and logs altogether. A subtle point is that indexed parameters are stored differently and may be hashed for dynamic types. For strings or arrays, the indexed value often becomes a hash in the filter. Finally, design your events with consistent field order to simplify parsing and ensure your client libraries know whether fields are indexed or not. What three fields would you index for your most common queries?

Understanding gas implications helps you choose the most efficient error reporting in production. require and revert both revert execution and refund unused gas; they are appropriate for expected user-facing failures. However, using string messages repeatedly across functions can increase transaction size and raise gas costs when failures occur. Custom errors are more gas-efficient because they encode a selector and parameters rather than full strings. That efficiency matters when failures are common or messages are long. assert is different: it indicates an internal bug and consumes all remaining gas when it fails, making failures loud and expensive. Use assert sparingly. Events also have gas costs: logs are cheaper than storage but are still not free. Keep event payloads minimal and index only commonly-filtered fields. A practical best practice is to use require or revert with short messages during development, then refactor frequent failure messages into custom errors before production, and always emit concise events. Tests should assert both expected reverts and emitted events so you can measure gas and confirm behavior. Which parts of your contract will you measure and optimize for gas?

When designing events and state changes, deciding whether to emit before or after a state modification impacts how logs are interpreted. A common guideline is to emit events after state changes so logs reflect the final confirmed state. For example, after reducing a balance and transferring funds, emit Withdrawal with the new balance to show the finished state. However, some events like OwnershipTransferred are sometimes emitted before assignment so the event can include the previous owner as well as the new owner; both approaches are valid if used consistently and documented. Inconsistent timing can confuse users and make debugging harder: if you emit before the final update and a subsequent operation reverts, the log may suggest an action that didn't complete. Always design event order to match how off-chain clients expect to reconstruct state and be explicit in your contract comments. For critical flows, include a test that checks both the state and the emitted event in the same transaction to ensure they align. Finally, if you must emit prior to a state change for context, ensure the event communicates that and include both old and new values when helpful. The Escrow contract is an excellent hands-on example to apply error handling and events. Start with clear state: depositor, beneficiary, arbiter, amount, and a boolean isReleased. The constructor assigns depositor to msg. sender and requires non-zero addresses for beneficiary and arbiter. These checks use require to validate input at deployment. Important invariants include that isReleased is false until funds are moved and that only the arbiter can release or refund the escrow. Protect these invariants using custom errors to provide compact, expressive failure signals such as NotArbiter and EscrowAlreadyReleased. Architecturally, keep the contract small and focused: deposit sets amount and emits FundsDeposited, release transfers the amount to beneficiary, sets isReleased to true and emits FundsReleased, and refund mirrors that flow back to the depositor. Remember to ensure correct order: change state before transfer where appropriate or vice versa based on reentrancy considerations and safety patterns. Document the role checks and event emission order so off-chain clients interpret logs correctly. As you implement, think about tests that assert that only the depositor can deposit and only the arbiter can trigger release or refund.

Let's walk through the deposit, release, and refund functions for a secure Escrow. The deposit function is payable and should only accept Ether from the depositor. Use a custom error NotDepositor(msg. sender) if msg. sender is not the depositor and ZeroAmount() if msg. value equals zero. After setting amount = msg. value, emit a FundsDeposited event with depositor, beneficiary, and amount. The release function must require that msg. sender is the arbiter and that the escrow is not already released; use NotArbiter and EscrowAlreadyReleased custom errors for clarity. Set isReleased to true and transfer the amount to beneficiary, then emit FundsReleased. The refund function mirrors release but sends funds back to the depositor and emits FundsRefunded. In implementation, checking and setting state before external calls helps limit reentrancy risks. Emit events to make the transitions observable for off-chain systems. Tests should assert that the correct custom error is reverted for invalid calls and that the proper event is emitted on success. By making errors typed and events indexed, you improve both gas efficiency and testability. Which of these checks will you unit-test first to build confidence?

This section highlights frequent errors and how to avoid them. First, don't over-rely on assert for input checks. Using assert where user input could fail wastes gas and miscommunicates the nature of the failure. Second, don't omit error messages or custom errors — cryptic reverts make debugging and user support difficult. Third, avoid putting sensitive data in events; logs are public and permanent. Fourth, be mindful of event order: emitting an event before a state change that later reverts can mislead off-chain systems. Fifth, avoid indexing unnecessary fields; indexing increases gas costs and log size. A practical safety note is to test not only that functions succeed but that they fail with the correct custom error and emit the intended event when successful. When refactoring from string messages to custom errors, update tests to check for the error selector or use tooling that decodes custom error reverts. Also measure gas for hot paths: repeated revert messages or large event payloads can raise transaction costs over heavy usage. Finally, maintain consistent documentation for your event schema and error types so consumers and auditors can rely on stable signals. Let's summarize the essential ideas to remember. First, require and revert are your tools for expected input or permission checks and refund remaining gas on failure. Use them for user-facing validations. Second, assert is reserved for internal invariants that should never fail; a failure consumes remaining gas and indicates a bug. Third, custom errors give you compact, typed reverts that save gas and improve programmatic handling of failures. Fourth, events are the cost-effective way to communicate state changes to off-chain clients; index up to three fields and keep payloads concise. Finally, test both failures and logs: assert custom errors in negative tests and confirm emitted events and resulting state in positive flows. These practices together produce safer, cheaper, and more observable smart contracts. A quick reference to keep handy while coding: 1) Validate with require or revert for expected external failures and refund unused gas; prefer concise messages in development and custom errors in production. 2) Use assert only for invariants that should never be false; a failed assert consumes all remaining gas and signals a code bug. 3) Emit events with indexed parameters for off-chain clients, keeping payloads minimal and avoiding sensitive data. Together these reminders help you build contracts that are efficient, debuggable, and observable. When you write tests, assert both the expected custom error on failure and the emitted events on success. That combination produces robust, maintainable smart contracts that integrate smoothly with dApps.
